head:
Seniors · Independence

Staying independent after 65: strength, balance, falls

After 65, the point is no longer to break a record. It is to keep getting up, walking, getting home and carrying your shopping without help. This article links simple tests to those everyday actions, shows what the studies prove and what they do not prove, then ends with what you can put in place.

The question

Take two tests. The first: count how many times you stand up from a chair in 30 seconds. The second: time 4 metres of walking at your usual pace. It looks like child's play. Yet doctors use them to estimate the risk of falling, the risk of losing independence, and even lifespan.

What changes after 65 is the nature of the goal. A 30-year-old athlete wants to go faster. At 70 or 80, the right measure is the margin: the gap between what your body can do and what your daily life asks of it. Getting up from the toilet, stepping off the bus, crossing before the light changes, recovering from a stumble. While the margin exists, you do not notice it. When it disappears, you fall or you stop going out.

The question

Do simple tests of strength, balance and walking really predict loss of independence and falls after 65? From what thresholds, and can you act on these numbers or only observe them?

Two other articles in this series cover neighbouring subjects: the article “How the body ages” explains which abilities decline with age, and “Getting up from the floor: what does this movement say about your health?” deals with the movement of getting up from the floor. Here, we do not repeat them. We start from daily life and work back up to the numbers.

What is at stake

The first stake is the fall itself. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), one person in four aged 65 and over falls each year, and one fall in five causes a serious injury, such as a fracture or a head injury. More than 3 million older adults are treated in emergency departments every year in the United States for a non-fatal fall.4 In France, the 2024 barometer indicates that nearly one person in five, all ages combined, reports a fall in the last 12 months; among 65 to 79-year-olds, 40% of falls lead to medical care.1

The second stake is silent: fewer than half of the Medicare beneficiaries who fell during the year told a doctor about it.4 An ability that declines does not hurt. A slower walk or a harder time getting up triggers no alarm. The first visible sign is often the fall, which is to say the moment when it is too late to act beforehand.

The third stake is independence in the strict sense: being able to walk outside on your own. In the LIFE trial (step 6), the endpoint is neither death nor fracture, but the loss of the ability to walk 400 metres.14

The fourth stake is collective: falls cost Medicare more than 31 billion dollars a year4 and, in France, nearly 2 billion euros a year according to the Cour des comptes (France's Court of Audit), part of it avoidable.1

This subject cannot be left unanswered: if simple movements predict the risk, ignoring them deprives you of a free signal; if they predict nothing reliable, relying on them puts you under pressure for nothing.
rest:
The demonstration

The reasoning goes from the broadest to the most precise: the whole population, one movement (walking), what the tests measure in everyday movements, the thresholds by age and sex, the objections, then what the trials show when we try to change the trajectory.

Step 1Risk does not rise gently with age, it soars

Claim: after 65, falling becomes a major public health problem, and the older we get, the steeper the curve.

Santé publique France tracks falls among people aged 65 and over. In 2024, the standardised hospitalisation rate is 1,198 per 100,000 people (+20.5% compared with 2019) and the death rate is 138 per 100,000 (+18%).2 “Standardised” means that population ageing does not distort the comparison. Mortality from falls even rose faster than the 2015-2019 trend, while all-cause mortality was lower in 2024 than in 2019.2

These averages hide a very clear gradient. And since fewer than one person in two talks to their doctor about it,4 we need a marker that does not wait for the accident.

Between 65 and 85, the severity of falls changes scale

Standardised rates in 2024, among people aged 65 and over in France. The 65 to 74 group is the reference (1). Ratios of 8.6 for hospitalisation and 29 for death, as given by the source. Source: Santé publique France.2

What this means

A person aged 85 and over is about 9 times more likely to be hospitalised after a fall than a person aged 65 to 74, and 29 times more likely to die from one. That mortality climbs faster than hospitalisation suggests that a very old body copes less well with the same blow; this is one reading, and the source does not explain it. Keep what is demonstrated: the risk is not spread evenly, it is concentrated late, which leaves years to act beforehand. Women are hospitalised more often, while men die proportionally more.2

The authorities have responded: the national anti-fall plan, launched in 2022, aimed for a 20% reduction. A trade press article notes that it is struggling to reverse the trend, and points out that only 20% of 50 to 79-year-olds reported regular physical activity in 2024.3

Step 2Walking speed sums up the state of the body

Claim: the time you take to walk a few metres at your usual pace is associated with your lifespan, well beyond age alone.

The reference study is that of Stéphanie Studenski and colleagues, published in JAMA in 2011. They pooled 9 cohorts, 34,485 adults aged 65 and over (mean age 73.5 years, mean speed 0.92 metres per second), followed for between 6 and 21 years. 17,528 died during follow-up.5

The key result: each additional 0.1 m/s of speed is associated with a 12% lower risk of death (risk ratio 0.88; confidence interval 0.87 to 0.90). After adjustment for sex, BMI, smoking, blood pressure, diseases, previous hospitalisations and self-reported health, the ratio stays at 0.90 (0.89 to 0.91).5 In practice, 0.1 m/s corresponds to half a second over 4 metres: 5.0 seconds at 0.8 m/s, 4.4 seconds at 0.9 m/s (derived calculation). Half a second over a short corridor is associated with about 10% lower risk.

The authors also estimated the 10-year survival of a 75-year-old according to speed.

At 75, walking speed separates very different fates

Predicted 10-year survival, at age 75, from the slowest to the fastest of the speeds studied. Figures from the study abstract. The intermediate figures were not read. Source: Studenski et al., JAMA, 2011.5

What this means

A 75-year-old man who walks very slowly has, according to the model, a 19% chance of being alive ten years later; walking very fast, 87%. For a woman, from 35% to 91%. The gap is about 4.6-fold in men and 2.6-fold in women (calculated ratios). Walking is not the cause: it is a marker of general condition. The authors do not detail the physiology; the common hypothesis is that walking engages legs, balance, heart, lungs and brain at the same time. It is a hypothesis.

Two benchmarks, reported by a trade press account: 0.8 m/s corresponds to median life expectancy for age and sex; from 1.2 m/s, predicted survival becomes “exceptional”.6 But “0.8 metres per second” means nothing to anyone: what is that figure worth in daily life? That is the subject of step 3.

Step 3From number to movement: what the tests really measure

Claim: the tests used in geriatrics are timed everyday movements, and their score is associated with loss of independence.

The most widely used battery is called the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB). It has three parts, each scored from 0 to 4, for a total of 0 to 12: holding balance (feet side by side, then one foot slightly in front of the other, then in tandem, each for up to 10 seconds), walking 4 metres, and standing up from a chair five times as fast as possible.7,20 The usual interpretation: 10 to 12 corresponds to minimal limitation, 7 to 9 to mild, 4 to 6 to moderate, 0 to 3 to severe.7

Guralnik and colleagues showed in 1994, in more than 5,000 people aged 71 and over, that each test and the overall score are strongly linked to reported disabilities and predict short-term mortality and nursing home admission, even in those who reported almost no disability.8 Over 4 years, people scoring 4 to 6 had a 4.2 times higher risk of losing independence in basic activities of daily living than those scoring 10 to 12 (ratio of 1.6 for 7 to 9), after adjustment for age, sex and chronic diseases.7

Among 512 older patients (mean age 79.4) seen in a day hospital for an acute illness, 58% of those scoring 0 to 4 had lost independence in a basic activity at one year, versus 13% of those scoring 9 to 12; death affected 21% versus 6%.9 These are sick patients, not the general population.

Translated into movements (editorial reading, outside the studies):

  • The five chair stands: getting up from a kitchen seat, from the toilet, from a car bench seat, from an armchair.
  • The 4 metres of walking: crossing a room, a corridor, a pedestrian crossing as far as the middle.
  • The balance positions: standing on a narrow surface, turning round without catching yourself, putting on trousers while standing.

Let us link this to step 2 by converting the SPPB walking score into speed (4 metres divided by the time): more than 8.70 s gives 1 point, 6.21 to 8.70 s 2 points, 4.82 to 6.20 s 3 points, less than 4.82 s 4 points.7

The walking test scores low speeds, and stops early

Derived figures: speed = 4 m divided by the time for each SPPB score; 0.44 m/s = 400 m in 15 minutes (the limit of the LIFE trial). Thresholds of 0.8 and 1.2 m/s: Studenski. Sources: Puthoff 2008; Studenski 2011; Pahor et al. 2014.7,6,14

What this means

Three benchmarks, three situations. Around 0.44 m/s, you are at the limit of being able to walk 400 metres without help (the LIFE independence criterion). Around 0.8 m/s, the walking test gives 3 or 4 points but predicted survival is “average”. At 1.2 m/s and above, there is margin. The SPPB no longer distinguishes anyone above 0.83 m/s: a maximal score can hide a limited margin, which Puthoff describes as a ceiling effect in people who function well.7

If speed is a good marker, the next question is from what point a result should raise concern, and whether the threshold is the same for everyone.

Step 4Thresholds change with age and sex, and with who sets them

Claim: there is no single boundary between “well” and “frail”; thresholds depend on age, sex and the institution that publishes them.

Take the 30-second chair stand test, used in the CDC's STEADI programme. You sit in the middle of a chair without armrests, placed against a wall, arms crossed over your chest, and you count your complete stands in 30 seconds. If you have to use your arms to help, the score is 0. The “below average” thresholds (hence high fall risk according to the handout) vary with age and sex.10,11

The number of stands judged sufficient falls with age, and collapses after 90 in women

A score below the value in the chart is classed as “below average”. Values come from the CDC STEADI handout; the age norms are attributed by bpac NZ to Rikli and Jones (1999). Source: CDC, STEADI handout 2017; bpac NZ.10,11

What this means

A 62-year-old woman who manages 11 stands is below average (threshold 12); at 77, 10 stands are not (threshold 10). The same number does not have the same value. The margin narrows quickly: between ages 60-64 and 90-94, the threshold goes from 14 to 7 in men and from 12 to 4 in women. Above the threshold, you are not safe; below it, you need to look closely, not fear a predicted fall.

For walking, thresholds diverge. The Timed Up and Go consists of standing up from a chair, walking about 3 metres, turning round and sitting down again. The CDC, according to an insurer's page that cites them, use 12 seconds or more as a sign of higher risk.12 A sheet from the Haute Autorité de Santé (HAS) speaks of a mobility deficit from 20 seconds, a major one beyond 29, and judges abnormal a single-leg stance of less than 5 seconds (date of the sheet not given in the excerpt read).13

Two institutions, two thresholds, 12 seconds against 20. They do not measure the same level (fall risk on one side, mobility deficit on the other) and the conditions differ (the HAS uses three attempts after a practice attempt). Neither is “the right one”.

Step 5The objections: what these numbers do not say

Claim: everything above is an association, useful but limited, and we must look at what could distort it.

Objection 1: a slow walk may be the consequence of a disease, not an independent signal

This is reverse causation. A sick person walks more slowly and dies earlier, without the slowness being responsible. The authors of the 2011 study acknowledge this in the uses they propose: speed is mainly informative after 75 in people without limitation or with minor limitations, and less useful in those who are already disabled or dependent.6 Adjusting for diseases reduces the association (0.88 becomes 0.90) without making it disappear.5

Objection 2: “predicting” does not mean “predicting well”

The C-statistic measures the quality of a prediction: 0.5 equals a coin toss, 1.0 a perfect prediction. Adding walking speed to age and sex raises it from 0.690 to 0.741 for 5-year survival, and from 0.712 to 0.734 at 10 years.5 The gain is real but modest (0.05 and 0.02, derived): speed helps to flag, it does not replace a medical examination.

Objection 3: the data are old, heterogeneous, sometimes converted

The data date from 1986 to 2000, the cohorts differ greatly from one another (heterogeneity of 82.3%), walking distances varied (4 to 6 metres, or 8 or 15 feet, converted by formula) and the intervals are wide in the oldest.5 The authors call for validation on other data before clinical use.6

Objection 4: are three tests better than one?

Depending on the population, the answer changes. Among 316 Mexican Americans followed for 7 years, the SPPB added nothing to speed alone for predicting death.7 Among the 512 day-hospital patients, the three components slightly improve discrimination (0.67 versus 0.62 for death), with modest values (0.60 for hospitalisation).9 So do not rely on a single test, and do not expect one more test to change everything.

Objection 5: measurement noise

The SPPB has a standard error of measurement of 1.42 points. Its smallest clinically meaningful difference is 0.54 points for a change perceived as small and 1.34 for a substantial change.7 In other words, a single point of difference between two attempts may be noise; you need a clear gap, or several consistent measurements, to conclude.

What this means

Solid: these tests are associated with survival and loss of independence, even after adjustment. Fragile: the exact threshold of concern, the comparison between institutions, the value of an isolated number. Not demonstrated: that a bad number is the cause of the problem. The last step therefore changes in nature: we look at what happens when we try to change the trajectory.

Step 6Can the trajectory be changed? What the trials show

Claim: well-designed exercise programmes reduce falls and delay the loss of the ability to walk; not all exercises are equal.

The Cochrane review by Sherrington (2019) pools 108 randomised trials, 23,407 participants with a mean age of 76, 77% of them women. Its overall effect is detailed in the article “How the body ages”; what matters here is the difference by type of exercise.1617

Balance exercises reduce falls; walking alone remains uncertain

Fall rate ratio: 1 = no effect, below 1 = fewer falls. The bars show the 95% confidence interval. “Walking alone” result: 2 trials, 441 participants. Sources: Sherrington et al., Cochrane, 2019; abridged version in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.16,18

What this means

A ratio of 0.76 means about 24% fewer falls for balance and functional exercises (high certainty); 0.66, about 34% fewer, for combined programmes (moderate certainty). For walking alone, the interval (0.66 to 1.97) crosses 1: we do not know whether it reduces or increases falls. That does not make it useless; it says that these trials do not show it.1617

The benefit is also found, with lower certainty, for fall-related fractures (ratio 0.73; 0.56 to 0.95) and falls requiring medical care (0.61; 0.47 to 0.79); for falls leading to hospital, it is uncertain (0.78; 0.51 to 1.18).16 Adverse events, mostly muscular and minor, are reported in 27 trials; only one monitored them closely in both groups.16

One specific programme has been tested many times, the Otago programme (New Zealand): leg strengthening and balance of increasing difficulty, ankle weights of about 1 kg at the start, about 30 minutes three times a week, walking for up to 30 minutes at least twice a week, 4 to 5 home visits by a trained professional. Among women aged 80 and over, falls fell by 32% and fall injuries by 39% in one year; pooling four trials (1,016 people aged 65 to 97), by 35% each, with the clearest benefit after 80. Caveat: in people taking sleeping pills, the programme alone showed no effect.19 These figures come from a presentation document, not from the original articles.

But independence is not only about not falling: the LIFE trial tested a programme on the ability to walk itself.

A structured programme delays the loss of the ability to walk

1,635 people aged 70 to 89, sedentary, with an SPPB of 9 or less but able to walk 400 m; mean follow-up 2.6 years. Risk ratios: 0.82 (0.69 to 0.98) and 0.72 (0.57 to 0.91). Source: Pahor et al., JAMA, 2014 (abstract).14,15

What this means

A gap of 5.4 points (30.1% versus 35.5%), or about 1 person in 19 spared over 2.6 years (derived calculation). The effect is moderate, not a guarantee, and clearer for persistent loss (14.7% versus 19.8%). In the most frail subgroup (SPPB below 8, 44.7% of participants), the risk ratio is 0.81.15 To keep in mind: serious adverse events are slightly more frequent in the activity group (49.4% versus 45.7%; ratio 1.08, interval 0.98 to 1.20), without the difference being established.14

The programme included two sessions a week at a centre and three to four at home: 30 minutes of moderate walking a day, then 10 minutes each of leg strengthening with ankle weights, balance and flexibility.1415 In an exercise trial of 424 people cited by a review of the SPPB, the score gained 0.7 points more than with education alone: close to the threshold for a change perceived as small (0.54), far from the substantial change (1.34).7

The answer to the question

The question was: do simple tests predict loss of independence and falls, from what thresholds, and can you act? Here is the answer, with its level of certainty.

Solid. Falls are frequent and serious, and the risk soars between 65 and 85. Timed walking, chair stands and balance are associated with survival and loss of independence, even after adjustment. Balance and functional exercises, and even more so combined programmes, reduce falls in randomised trials.

Probable. A structured programme (walking, strengthening, balance, flexibility) delays the loss of the ability to walk (one trial, LIFE). The tests help to spot a shrinking margin, especially with several measurements spaced apart.

Not demonstrated. No single threshold is established (12 or 20 seconds on the Timed Up and Go, variable chair-stand thresholds). That raising your number reduces your risk precisely is not proven: the trials show the effect of a programme on events, not the value of a score. For climbing stairs and carrying a load, no source read provides a validated test: these movements matter for independence, and the page measures them only indirectly, through leg strength and power.

Independence is therefore played out on a margin, not on a record. Around 0.44 m/s, walking alone outside is threatened; around 0.8 m/s, you are average; at 1.2 m/s or more, you have reserve. The aim is not to reach 1.2 at all costs: it is not to let the margin melt away without knowing it.

What to put in place

The measurements depend on the page's test; adapt them to its protocol.

  1. Measure three movements, once, in a calm setting.The 30-second chair stand (chair against a wall, arms crossed, someone nearby), the 4-metre walk at your usual pace (speed = 4 divided by the time in seconds), and the Timed Up and Go or a single-leg stance. Compare with the age sheet in the step 4 chart, without seeing it as a verdict.11,12,13
  2. Record, then repeat every 3 to 6 months, in the same conditions.Same chair, same shoes, same time of day. A small gap proves nothing (step 5). This frequency is an editorial recommendation, without a source. The LIFE trial assessed participants every 6 months.15
  3. Work on balance and legs first.This is what reduces falls in the trials (0.76 for balance, 0.66 when strengthening is added).16 Dose observed in the programmes: about 30 minutes three times a week for Otago, with ankle weights of about 1 kg and increasing difficulty;19 two supervised sessions and three to four sessions at home for LIFE.14 Tai chi is an option.16
  4. Keep walking, without making it the only programme.It is part of LIFE and Otago; on its own, its effect on falls is uncertain.14,18
  5. Keep an eye on stairs and carrying loads, without making them a threshold.Climbing a floor without the handrail, carrying a bag of shopping for ten metres: these are observation markers, not validated tests. If one becomes difficult, bring it up in the conversation with your doctor.
  6. Talk to a professional.The HAS recommends asking every older person whether they fell in the previous year.13 A recent fall, dizziness, pain or the use of sleeping pills justify medical advice before increasing training: in Otago, the programme alone showed nothing in people taking sleeping pills.19

The earlier you take the first measurement, the more hindsight you have to see a slope.

What these figures do not say
  • Many of the figures on the tests come from old cohorts (1986-2000 for Studenski) or from particular populations (day-hospital patients, sedentary people at risk in LIFE): your results may differ.
  • The CDC, HAS and SPPB thresholds are not equivalent. The 12-second Timed Up and Go threshold is relayed by an insurer's page, not read in a CDC document.

Frequently asked questions

My score is below the threshold: am I in danger?

Not necessarily. A threshold signals a higher risk on average, not a predicted fall. Repeat the test at another time, in the same conditions, and if the result is confirmed, talk to a professional.10,7

I walk every day: is that enough?

Walking is part of effective programmes, but the Cochrane review does not establish that it reduces falls on its own (ratio 1.14, interval 0.66 to 1.97, 2 trials). The programmes that reduce falls add balance and functional exercises.16,18

Is it too late at 80?

Nothing in these studies suggests it. The Otago programme is most effective after 80, and the mean age in LIFE was 78.9 years (from 70 to 89).19,15 That does not guarantee the same result for you.

Can a test make me fall?

It is a risk to take seriously: chair against a wall, someone next to you, and stop if you are at risk of falling, as the handout used in New Zealand specifies.11
